source.title: Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
source.authors: Bradley Brown; Jordan Juravsky; Ryan Ehrlich; Ronald Clark; Quoc V. Le; Christopher Ré; Azalia Mirhoseini

page_placements.theme: Sampling, ensembles, search and interaction provide conditional scaling gains

record.tranche_reason: The study measures inference-time sample count versus problem coverage, not held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or training compute, nor the training compute-optimal allocation in the claim versions. It draws an analogy to training scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for coverage scaling with inference-time samples. This is a related but different outcome from the training-loss and training-allocation claims. Its references to training scaling laws are background; they are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study scales inference-time samples per problem and measures task coverage (pass@k). It reports no held-out pretraining loss and does not vary or fit training parameters, tokens or compute. It does not test compute-optimal training allocation, architecture shape or training regimes. Training scaling laws appear only as motivation and analogy (Section 3, Related Work). Models of different sizes are compared, but only as coverage curves under repeated sampling. There is no fitted or tested claim that downstream performance is predictable from training scale or loss, so V6 is not tested either.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude three things. First, repeated sampling raises coverage across tasks and models over four orders of magnitude, often following an exponentiated power law that suggests inference-time scaling laws. Second, with automatic verifiers this lets weaker models beat stronger single-sample models, sometimes more cheaply. Third, without verifiers, majority voting and reward models plateau around 100 samples, leaving a growing gap to coverage.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales independent inference-time samples and measures task coverage; the original sources study pretraining loss and compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Coverage-curve fit and gains vary by model family and task. The authors specifically note that Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MiniF2F-MATH does not closely follow the exponentiated power-law fit; Pythia models on CodeContests have zero coverage even at 10,000 samples.

fits_no_version.finding: Coverage versus number of inference samples is approximated by c ≈ exp(a k^b) for most model-task pairs, with small fit errors (e.g. 0.002-0.03). The fit is poorer for Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MiniF2F-MATH, and the authors call these laws less exact than training laws.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time coverage under repeated sampling follows an exponentiated power law in sample count.

fits_no_version.finding: Repeated sampling raises coverage by large factors: Gemma-2B on CodeContests 0.02% to 7.1%; Pythia-160M on MATH 0.27% to 57%; Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10k. Majority vote and reward-model selection plateau near 100 samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated inference sampling increases coverage, but common selection methods do not scale with the sample budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Within the Pythia family on MATH, the fitted coefficient a rises with model size, from -7.59 at 70M to -3.92 at 12B (Figure 10). Same-family coverage curves are similar S-curves shifted horizontally (Figure 6). This is incidental and is not framed as a scale law.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a model family, inference-sampling coverage curves share slope and shift with model size.

record.problems: The paper describes the power-law fits as less exact than training scaling laws and notes a poor fit for Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MiniF2F-MATH. The reported results use task coverage and inference-time sample counts, so they do not establish any of the listed training-loss or training-allocation versions.
record.rows_left_out: No other fit rows or coverage rows were included. Appendix Figure 10 gives additional coverage-fit plots for more model-task settings, but the listed rows retain the explicit coefficient/error pairs from Figure 5 and numerical coverage changes stated in the text.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or training compute; not measured.
Extrapolation of training-loss fits from small to large runs; not attempted.
Compute-optimal parameter/token split for a training budget. The 8B vs 70B FLOP comparison (Figure 4) concerns inference compute, not training allocation.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count; not varied.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes. Repeated sampling at inference is not a training regime, and coverage is not loss.
Predictability of downstream performance from model scale or pretraining loss. Model sizes appear (Pythia 70M-12B) but no scale-performance law is fitted or tested.
Dependence of training-law exponents or allocations on setup and fitting choices; not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly unlinked (versions none), and the cannot_determine states are appropriate for this claim. The paper is not an original source. No verdicts are given because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or training compute.
Whether small training runs predict the loss of much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation for a fixed training-compute budget.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Whether the training-loss power-law form transfers to other modalities or training regimes. Inference-time repeated sampling is not tested as a training regime.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of training-loss exponents or training compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.

tranche.reason: The study measures inference-time sampling coverage and verification, without testing or using the catalog's claims about training-scale loss, allocation, architecture or downstream predictability from training scale.

source_check.notes: The statement is supported by the introduction and Section 4.1. Its cited rows r9 and r10 concern different models and datasets; only r11 records its Llama-3-8B-Instruct coverage numbers.
